content: 1. Ridis G, Tsochatzis E, Hardke S, and Wedemeyer H conducted a systematic review in 2014 to identify barriers to care and treatment for patients with chronic viral hepatitis in Europe. Their findings were published in Liver International. 2. Feeney ER and Chung RT discussed antiviral treatment options for hepatitis C in a 2014 article published in BMJ. They highlighted advancements in therapeutic approaches. 3. Pawlotsky JM reviewed new therapies for hepatitis C, including available tools, strategies, and challenges, in a 2014 article in Gastroenterology. This work emphasized the evolving landscape of hepatitis C management. 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) released guidelines in 2014 for the screening, care, and treatment of individuals with hepatitis C infection. These guidelines provide a framework for improving global health outcomes related to hepatitis C. 5. Soriano V, Labarga P, Fernández-Montero JV, Benito JM, Poveda E, Rallón N, and colleagues examined the impact of direct-acting antivirals on the management of hepatitis C in a 2013 study published in Antiviral Research. They described the transformative effects of these medications on treatment paradigms. 6. Duskova D and Darebnicek L evaluated nucleic acid testing for hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in blood donors at the General University Hospital in Prague. Their findings, published in Acta Virologica in 2014, underscored the importance of accurate diagnostic methods in blood safety. 7. Khuroo MS, Khuroo NS, and Khuroo MS conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2015 to assess the diagnostic accuracy of point-of-care tests for hepatitis C virus infection. Their work, published in PLOS One, highlighted the potential of these tests in improving access to diagnosis. 8. Shivkumar S, Peeling R, Jafari Y, Joseph L, and Pant Pai N performed a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2012 to evaluate the accuracy of rapid and point-of-care screening tests for hepatitis C. Their findings, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, demonstrated the utility of these tests in diverse clinical settings. 9. Whiting PF, Rutjes AW, Westwood ME, Mallett S, Deeks JJ, Reitsma JB, and colleagues developed the QUADAS-2 tool in 2011 to assess the quality of diagnostic accuracy studies. This tool, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, provides a standardized approach for evaluating diagnostic research. 10. Bossuyt PM, Reitsma JB, Bruns DE, Gatsonis CA, Glasziou PP, Irwig LM, and colleagues introduced the STARD statement in 2003 to improve the reporting of diagnostic accuracy studies. Their work, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, aimed to enhance transparency and reproducibility in diagnostic research. 11. Advances in hepatitis C virus (HCV) detection technology have created opportunities to improve screening, referral, and treatment. A systematic review conducted in 2015 compared the accuracy of qualitative nucleic acid testing (NAT) methods with quantitative NAT methods for detecting and quantifying HCV RNA. The review found that qualitative NAT assays are at least 10 times more sensitive than quantitative assays, with detection limits as low as 10–15 IU/mL compared to 600–1100 IU/mL for quantitative assays. However, newer quantitative platforms now match the sensitivity of qualitative assays, with linear quantification ranges between 12 and 108 IU/mL. 12. The review emphasized the importance of rapid HCV detection to prevent disease progression to chronic stages. Both qualitative and quantitative NAT methods are essential for confirming active HCV infection, though research comparing these methods remains limited. The findings also highlighted the cost-effectiveness and accessibility of point-of-care (POC) devices for HCV viral load quantification, which are expected to improve access to HCV detection and treatment monitoring. 13. The systematic review identified gaps in the standardization of diagnostic test evaluations and the lack of detailed information on study populations. Despite these limitations, the review demonstrated the critical role of sensitive diagnostic assays in managing HCV infection, particularly in resource-limited settings. 14. The development of affordable POC devices capable of quantifying HCV viral load offers significant potential for improving access to care. These devices, which are portable and require minimal training, can be used outside laboratory settings and integrated into existing healthcare infrastructure. 15. The review concluded that leveraging investments in diagnostic platforms for other diseases, such as HIV, could support HCV control programs. Additionally, HCV antigen detection may serve as a surrogate marker for ongoing viral replication in settings where NAT assays are not affordable.
